title: She Scored 68 Off 36 Balls. India Still Lost by Five Runs.
excerpt: Richa Ghosh played the innings of the Women's T20 World Cup warm-ups — nine fours, two sixes, a strike rate of 189 — but India's top-order collapse made her heroics academic
body:
Richa Ghosh batted like she had a personal grudge against the English bowling attack. Sixty-eight runs off 36 balls. Nine boundaries. Two sixes. A strike rate of 188.88. It was, by every measure, the most explosive innings any Indian batter has played in this tournament cycle. And it still wasn't enough.

England Women beat India by five runs in their final warm-up match before the ICC Women's T20 World Cup at Sophia Gardens, Cardiff, on June 10. India were bowled out for 166 chasing 172, and the margin — five runs, one ball remaining — tells you exactly how close Ghosh came to pulling off a heist that had no business succeeding.

## The Collapse Before the Carnage

India's chase began in disaster. Smriti Mandhana, the team's most elegant stroke-player and the batter most likely to anchor an innings, lasted six balls for one run before Linsey Smith had her caught. Opening partner Shafali Verma hit 13 off 6 — aggressive, chaotic, quintessentially Shafali — before Issy Wong cleaned her up.

At 18 for 2 in the third over, India needed calm. What they got was competent mediocrity. Yastika Bhatia made 15 off 17, captain Harmanpreet Kaur managed 17 off 18, and Bharti Fulmali contributed 18 off 17. None of them were terrible. All of them were insufficient. These were survival innings in a match that demanded counterattack.

By the time Ghosh walked in at number six, India were 70 for 4 in the 10th over. The required rate was climbing past 10 an over. The sensible move would have been to bat deep, keep wickets in hand, hope for a late flurry. Ghosh chose violence instead.

## The Ghosh Innings

She started with a four off her third ball and never looked back. Her method was simple: anything in her arc got dispatched. She pulled Wong for six over midwicket. She drove Dean through extra cover. She reverse-swept Smith for four. The English bowlers, who had been moving through India's top order with casual efficiency, suddenly looked frantic.

The penultimate over, bowled by Wong, went for 21 runs — almost entirely off Ghosh's bat. India needed 17 off the final over. Ghosh hit a four and a six off consecutive deliveries from Linsey Smith, and for one delirious moment, 11 off 4 balls felt achievable.

Then Smith found the stumping. Ghosh, reaching for a delivery that wasn't quite there, was beaten by a ball that dipped and turned. Alice Capsey whipped off the bails. The innings was over. India's chase effectively died with it.

## Harmanpreet's Honest Assessment

"I think it's about partnerships," Harmanpreet said in the post-match press conference. "Only Richa played a blinder. In T20 cricket, you need a few partnerships in the middle, which we missed today."

The captain's candour was refreshing and necessary. India's problem wasn't their bowling — Shreyanka Patil took 2 for 29, and the attack kept England to 171 despite a late assault from Danielle Gibson (30 off 12). The problem was a batting lineup that, outside of Ghosh, collectively failed to impose itself on a very chaseable target.

## The England Side of the Scorecard

England's 171 for 6 was built on familiar foundations. Amy Jones (64 off 45) and Nat Sciver-Brunt (57 off 45) combined for a second-wicket partnership of 70 that gave the innings its spine. Sciver-Brunt survived a contentious not-out decision when she inside-edged a Shreyanka Patil delivery onto her boot, the ball popped up, and Ghosh took the catch. The umpire said not out. In a tournament game, DRS would have settled it. In a warm-up, it became the kind of talking point that festers.

Gibson's cameo at the death — 30 off 12 — pushed the total past 170 and ultimately proved the difference.

## What It Means for the Tournament

India open their World Cup campaign against Pakistan on June 14 at Edgbaston. The rivalry needs no introduction, and Harmanpreet's team will carry the confidence of knowing they have a match-winner in Ghosh who can singlehandedly change a game's trajectory in 36 balls.

But they'll also carry the worry that their top order — Mandhana, Shafali, Yastika, Harmanpreet herself — looked brittle against quality bowling. England's attack wasn't even at full strength. When India face the likes of Australia, South Africa, or a fired-up Pakistan, the margin for top-order failure shrinks to nothing.

For NRIs in the UK — and there will be thousands at Edgbaston, Old Trafford, and The Oval during this tournament — the warm-up offered both thrill and anxiety. The thrill was Ghosh. The anxiety was everything else.

India beat West Indies in their other warm-up match, so the preparation hasn't been entirely bleak. But the Pakistan game will demand the kind of collective intent that was missing in Cardiff. Ghosh proved she can win a match on her own. The question is whether she'll have to.
author: Diaspora Desk
